query: Single-phase ZrB2 benefits from strong Zr–B and B–B interactions and a high melting point, but it requires preparation temperatures above 2300 °C and does not readily meet application requirements on its own. Earlier studies sought to lower the required temperature, yet the resulting materials remained vulnerable to high-temperature oxidation or liquid plating-metal corrosion, while reported preparation temperatures generally remained above 1700 °C. Under the constraints of lower-temperature manufacture, adequate strength and structural integrity, oxidation durability, and prolonged service in a liquid plating bath, what single intervention could overcome these limitations? Provide one hypothesis specifying the intervention, mechanism, predicted outcome compared with single-phase ZrB2 and prior lower-temperature specimens, applicable preparation and service boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled experiment evaluating final body quality, structural integrity, oxidation, and liquid-metal corrosion that would falsify the hypothesis if its predictions were not observed.

generation.hypothesis: The addition of a refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) to ZrB2 can improve its high-temperature oxidation resistance and structural integrity, while reducing the required preparation temperature.
generation.intervention: Addition of a RHEA, such as NbTaHfTiZr or AlCrMnNbTiV, to ZrB2
generation.conditions: High-temperature environment, above 1500 °C, in the presence of liquid heavy metals
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a disordered BCC solid-solution structure and the presence of refractory elements
generation.mechanism: The RHEA addition can improve the oxidation resistance of ZrB2 by forming a protective oxide layer and reducing the diffusion of oxygen into the material. The refractory elements in the RHEA can also improve the high-temperature stability and structural integrity of the material.
generation.predicted_outcome: Improved high-temperature oxidation resistance and structural integrity, reduced preparation temperature, and enhanced overall performance of ZrB2 in high-temperature applications
generation.boundary: Temperature range: 1500-2000 °C, environment: high-temperature oxidation and liquid heavy metal corrosion
generation.uncertainty: The exact composition and processing conditions of the RHEA addition, as well as the potential interactions between the RHEA and ZrB2, are uncertain and require further investigation

falsification_experiment.design: High-temperature oxidation and corrosion testing of ZrB2 with and without RHEA addition
measurements: Oxidation resistance, structural integrity, and microstructure analysis
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the RHEA addition does not improve the high-temperature oxidation resistance and structural integrity of ZrB2, the hypothesis is falsified

cited_evidence.text: The NbTaHfTiZr HEA has received a lot of interests among all RHEAs, since it has a totally disordered BCC solid-solution structure with a melting point of about 1800 °C [,]. At normal temperature and cryogenic temperatures, the NbTaHfTiZr RHEA combines excellent strength and ductility []. The NbTaHfTiZrV0.5 RHEA based on this alloy not only maintains excellent room-temperature plasticity but also further improves its strength and has a good cold workability []. In order to explore the potential of the NbTaHfTiZrV0.5 RHEA for high-temperature applications, it is very necessary to study its mechanical properties at high temperatures. Here, we explore the mechanical properties of the NbTaHfTiZrV0.5 alloy from RT to 1227 K and analyze its microscopic deformation mechanism. At the same time, we construct the constitutive equation of this alloy through a stress–strain curve in a deformation temperature range of 873–1173 K and a 0.001–0.1 s−1 strain-rate range and quantify the relationship between the strength and temperature.

Hardness and oxidation measurements were conducted using all six single-phase high-entropy diborides (HEB #1-#5 and #7) and six individual metal diboride benchmarking specimens (HfB2, ZrB2, TaB2, NbB2, TiB2, and CrB2) that were made by the same HEBM and SPS fabrication method using the same processing parameters, with one exception that CrB2 was sintered at lower temperature of 1800 °C because its substantially lower melting (and therefore sintering) temperature. MoB2 was not examined because it is not a thermodynamically stable phase (and will decompose to MoB and Mo2B5) below 1500 °C. Hardness measurements were performed with a Vickers’ diamond indenter at 200 kgf/mm2 with a hold time of 15 seconds. The indentations were examined for conformation with the ASTM C1327. The indentations averaged 20–25 μm in width during the testing. Multiple measurements were performed at different locations of each specimen; the mean and standard deviation are reported.
